newsitem.title: USA: Fla. utility to build coal-limestone power unit.
newsitem.headline: Fla. utility to build coal-limestone power unit.

text.p: Lakeland, Fla., using a $195 million Department of Energy grant, plans to ring in the new century with an innovative power unit fired by an unlikely mixture of coal and limestone.
The 170 megawatt unit, to start construction in late 1998 at its McIntosh power plant in central Florida, will also cut toxic emissions and costs to its customers, a company spokesman said.
"The bulk of the clean-up is done while burning the coal. The limestone traps those chemicals before they're emitted. It moves it out in a different matter," he said.
The exact reduction in emissions of sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide and particulate matter was not yet available by the company, but he said they would be reduced to levels below federal requirements.
About 157 megawatts of power will be available in late 2000, and the rest will be added two years later, he said.

The federal grant, issued October 29 as part of the Clean Coal Technology Program, represents 50 percent of the construction costs and 50 percent of operating costs over a four-year demonstration period.
The City of Lakeland's Department of Electric & Water Utility, Florida's third largest municipal utility with a customer base of more than 104,000, will fund the remainder.
The new technology, known as Pressurized Circulating Fluidized Bed, was developed by Foster Wheeler Development Corp and Westinghouse Electric Corp.
Testing of this process has been performed at a research facility in New Jersey and small pilot plants in Alabama and Finland.
The McIntosh facility already has three units generating about 656 megawatts of electricity.
Units 1 and 2 can be fired by oil or natural gas. Unit 3, partly owned by Orlando Utilities Commission, runs on coal but can also burn diesel or oil.

Lakeland Electric & Water also operates the Larsen Power Plant, which generates about 192 megawatts (MW), using natural gas and/or oil. Also at the plant are three peaking units, each with a 13 MW capacity.
The utility has estimated that by 1999 it will need an additional 75-100 MW of power to meet demand.
